quote: No, because there is no experiment you can perform yourself to verify it.
content: By this criterion the 1919 eclipse expedition, which the sequence presents two essays later as the paradigm test of a scientific theory, was not science: it was a one-off observation of a historical event that no reader can rerun. The same goes for the Chicxulub impact, the Big Bang, continental drift, and every phylogeny. Historical sciences establish claims through convergent "smoking gun" traces rather than repeatable experiment and are not epistemically inferior for it (Cleland 2002). The essay's definition, science as reproducible generalization, is a philosophy-of-physics stipulation that excludes most of geology, astronomy and evolutionary biology and is not the one working scientists in those fields use.

quote: Science is the publicly reproducible knowledge of humankind.
content: Reproducible in principle, and, as the following decade showed, mostly never reproduced. When one hundred published psychology findings were rerun, 36 percent replicated (Open Science Collaboration 2015); in cancer biology, about half of tested effects replicated at much smaller sizes (Errington et al. 2021). In practice science runs on trust in testimony, not personal verification; almost no scientist can verify the results they build on (Hardwig 1991; Shapin 1994, A Social History of Truth, book, no DOI). The essay draws its line between science and history at reproducibility. The replication crisis showed that the "protected belief pool" was protected by the same thing as Plutarch: nobody had checked.

quote: why bother to run the experiment?
content: The essay says it is "dangerous" to hold a scientific belief about an untested prediction, and asks why one would run the experiment if the answer were known. Two essays later, Einstein's Arrogance argues that a competent theorist should be "damn sure" of the result before the test, and that this is the correct epistemic state. The two positions cannot both be the sequence's view. The actual answer to "why bother" is the value of information: with confidence below one, an experiment still has positive expected value (Good 1967), and it also tests the auxiliary assumptions and instruments, which is where most surprises come from. The essay reaches for a definition of "scientific" that makes prediction unscientific, which it admits "seems perverse," rather than notice that the puzzle dissolves once belief comes in degrees.

quote: only open knowledge counts as the public, reproducible knowledge pool of humankind
content: This 2007 proposal was largely enacted. Open access grew from a minority to a plurality of new articles, funders mandated it, and the results were not what the essay implies. Reliability tracks methods, not access: the replication failures of the 2010s occurred in open and closed journals alike, and the author-pays model that financed open access created thousands of predatory journals that publish anything for a fee (Grudniewicz et al. 2019). "Can we trust a result if people must pay to criticize it?" turned out to be the wrong question; the relevant one was whether anyone had tried to reproduce it, which access did not change. The essay conflates a distribution problem with an epistemic one.
